text: Background: Pedestrian experience depends on local environmental conditions that are often averaged or omitted in citywide datasets; the present study addressed this issue through footway obstruction in a historic centre. Temporary obstructions such as café terraces, delivery pallets and construction hoardings intermittently reduce walking space but are invisible to static inventories. This work tested a sensing-based workflow for footway obstruction in a historic centre without relying solely on a pre-existing neighbourhood score so that local conditions remained interpretable after aggregation. Methods: A network of low-power ultrasonic and optical units was installed along a heritage street to detect lateral encroachment onto the footway at fifteen-minute intervals over six months. Detected obstruction width was validated against periodic manual measurement. In the final processing stage, the retained observations were georeferenced and attached to the pedestrian network to avoid masking local differences through area-wide averaging. Before interpreting footway obstruction in a historic centre, the authors screened the measurements for missing values, implausible readings and periods of incomplete spatial coverage. Results: The segment-level estimates were compared between neighbouring links with otherwise similar network characteristics to determine whether the sensed attribute captured meaningful local variation. Encroachment exceeded one metre during 19 percent of daytime hours, concentrated in the late afternoon. Conclusions: At network scale, taken together, the results demonstrate the value of direct, pedestrian-scale measurement for representing a dimension of walkability that is poorly captured by conventional proxies, providing a practical basis for future work on footway obstruction in a historic centre.

text: Microclimatic conditions can change within tens of metres, making neighbourhood-average temperature a poor proxy for the thermal environment experienced during walking; the present study addressed this issue through bluetooth and infrared counting to characterise pedestrian volumes on a waterfront promenade. The analysis tested the feasibility of retaining the variables underlying bluetooth and infrared counting to characterise pedestrian volumes on a waterfront promenade as route-level evidence under real-world conditions. Understanding temporal patterns of pedestrian use supports management of public space. Infrared beam counters and Bluetooth detectors were deployed at eight gateways along a waterfront promenade for one year. Counts were corrected for device-specific detection rates estimated through manual calibration sessions. Once the observations had been screened, the retained observations were georeferenced and attached to the pedestrian network so that short-distance variation remained visible. The segment-level estimates were compared against relevant guidance thresholds and complementary streetscape variables to determine whether the sensed attribute captured meaningful local variation. Seasonal, weekly and diurnal profiles were derived and related to weather records, revealing strong sensitivity of promenade use to thermal conditions and precipitation. Because bluetooth and infrared counting to characterise pedestrian volumes on a waterfront promenade may vary both spatially and temporally, the two sources of variation were examined separately before producing route-level summaries. From a pedestrian-planning perspective, the results support the use of pedestrian-scale thermal measurements when prioritising shade, material or route interventions under hot-weather conditions, with particular relevance to bluetooth and infrared counting to characterise pedestrian volumes on a waterfront promenade.

text: Kerb geometry determines whether a crossing is negotiable by users with reduced mobility. Crossing conditions are a critical component of pedestrian mobility because route continuity depends on both infrastructure provision and operational performance, a concern directly relevant to depth camera assessment of step height and kerb geometry at pedestrian crossings. The investigation assessed whether direct observations could provide sufficient spatial detail for depth camera assessment of step height and kerb geometry at pedestrian crossings at a resolution suitable for pedestrian-environment assessment. A handheld depth camera was used to capture the crossing geometry at 340 intersections, from which kerb height, ramp gradient and gutter depth were reconstructed. Measurements were compared with manual gauge readings on a validation subset, showing millimetre-level agreement. Once the observations had been screened, the retained observations were georeferenced and attached to the pedestrian network so that persistent spatial patterns could be distinguished from transient variation. Nearly half of surveyed crossings exceeded the maximum permissible kerb height, and non-compliance was more frequent on secondary streets. The route-level indicators were compared across contrasting route types and local environmental contexts to separate persistent environmental differences from short-term fluctuations. For depth camera assessment of step height and kerb geometry at pedestrian crossings, reference observations were kept separate from the main processing wherever possible so that agreement could be evaluated independently. At network scale, the resulting measures can be incorporated into route-level accessibility and safety assessment rather than treating all mapped crossings as equivalent, with particular relevance to depth camera assessment of step height and kerb geometry at pedestrian crossings.

To preserve the practical meaning of measuring visual permeability and enclosure in residential streets, results were reported in the original measurement units as well as in any derived indicator. text: Background: Many dimensions of streetscape quality are inherently visual and are poorly represented in conventional two-dimensional geospatial datasets, a concern directly relevant to segmenting street-level imagery to assess weather protection along pedestrian routes. The analysis of association between neighbourhood environment perceptions and self-reported walking in older adults was repeated under alternative spatial aggregation rules because the chosen unit can materially affect urban associations. Residents possess detailed knowledge of everyday mobility constraints. Accordingly, focus groups and walking interviews explored safety, drainage and social barriers. Participants emphasised harassment and seasonal flooding. In the modelling stage, the principal explanatory variables were entered into the statistical or machine-learning model and performance was assessed against a simpler baseline. The predictive results were assessed under alternative sampling or feature definitions to assess robustness and practical relevance. In practical terms, the evidence is qualitative and no sensor-based measurement was undertaken. Interpretation of qualitative study of barriers to walking in informal settlements followed model evaluation so that feature importance did not substitute for predictive or statistical validity. The available data constrained the temporal and spatial coverage of the analysis, although sensitivity checks produced similar qualitative conclusions before generalising findings about qualitative study of barriers to walking in informal settlements. Overall, the study demonstrates the usefulness of the selected data and analytical method for its target urban application, while keeping the interpretation centred on qualitative study of barriers to walking in informal settlements.

text: Seasonal terraces alter footway capacity and pedestrian movement. Pedestrian experience depends on local environmental conditions that are often averaged or omitted in citywide datasets; the present study addressed this issue through time-of-flight monitoring of outdoor dining expansion. The investigation evaluated whether direct observations could provide sufficient spatial detail for time-of-flight monitoring of outdoor dining expansion so that local conditions remained interpretable after aggregation. The proposed workflow combined field acquisition and analysis: time-of-flight sensors measured the occupied envelope of tables and chairs at regular intervals, while cameras recorded pedestrian diversion behaviour. Encroachment exceeded permitted boundaries most often during evening peaks and at corners. For spatial analysis, sensor outputs were aggregated at route-segment level rather than neighbourhood level so that persistent spatial patterns could be distinguished from transient variation. The study provides continuous evidence for managing shared sidewalk space. The resulting measurements were analysed against relevant guidance thresholds and complementary streetscape variables to evaluate the extent to which the measure represented a distinct dimension of the walking environment. For time-of-flight monitoring of outdoor dining expansion, reference observations were kept separate from the main processing wherever possible so that agreement could be evaluated independently. Overall, the study provides a repeatable method for adding fine-grained environmental evidence to pedestrian network assessment and intervention planning, with particular relevance to time-of-flight monitoring of outdoor dining expansion.

text: The study modelled associations relevant to bibliometric mapping of walkability research themes with calibration and validation tailored to the target outcome. Many studies concerned with cities or mobility use technologies that also appear in pedestrian research, although the measured outcome may be different, which is especially important when considering bibliometric mapping of walkability research themes. The field spans public health, transport and urban design. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: publication metadata, keywords and citation networks were analysed to identify thematic clusters. Technology-based assessment emerged as a growing topic. After preprocessing, the principal explanatory variables were entered into the statistical or machine-learning model with sensitivity analyses used to test the stability of the main result. The analytical results were examined under alternative sampling or feature definitions to determine whether the proposed approach improved on established methods. The study maps literature rather than sensing pedestrian environments. The analysis of bibliometric mapping of walkability research themes was repeated under alternative spatial aggregation rules because the chosen unit can materially affect urban associations. The available data constrained the temporal and spatial coverage of the analysis, although sensitivity checks produced similar qualitative conclusions for applications involving bibliometric mapping of walkability research themes. Taken together, the study demonstrates the usefulness of the selected data and analytical method for its target urban application, supporting the study's primary application involving bibliometric mapping of walkability research themes.
